quiz_ct:10.q: The cells containing dark ingested particles are derived from which blood cell?
quiz_ct:10.alt: Light micrograph of cells, some containing dark particles

quiz_ct:11.q: What is this cell type called when it resides in the liver?
quiz_ct:11.r: Macrophage (abundant lysosomes, faculty slide 977): Kupffer cell in liver.
quiz_ct:11.alt: Electron micrograph of a cell with many dense vesicles

quiz_ct:12.q: The cell at the arrow is derived from which cell?
quiz_ct:12.r: Plasma cell: derived from stimulated B lymphocytes.
quiz_ct:12.alt: Blood smear with an arrow pointing at one cell

quiz_ct:13.q: What is the main secretory product of this cell?
quiz_ct:13.r: Plasma cell (faculty slide 974): abundant RER, synthesizes immunoglobulins.
quiz_ct:13.alt: Light and electron micrographs of one cell type

quiz_ct:14.q: Release of the granules in this cell is triggered when antigen binds to which surface-bound molecule?
quiz_ct:14.r: Mast cell: surface IgE receptors bind IgE; second exposure cross-links and degranulates.
quiz_ct:14.alt: Electron micrograph of a cell packed with dark granules

quiz_ct:15.q: Which mast cell product increases capillary permeability?
quiz_ct:15.r: Histamine: vasodilator, increases capillary permeability, bronchoconstrictor.

quiz_ct:16.q: Which mast cell mediator is made from membrane phospholipids after activation?
quiz_ct:16.r: Phospholipases act on membrane phospholipids to produce leukotrienes (not preformed).

quiz_ct:19.q: In a proteoglycan aggregate, the link protein attaches the core protein to which molecule?
quiz_ct:19.r: Link protein joins core protein to hyaluronan.

quiz_ct:2.q: The dermis and the capsules of glands are composed of which type of connective tissue?
quiz_ct:2.r: Dense irregular: dermis, gland capsules, periosteum.

quiz_ct:20.q: Which glycoprotein is secreted by epithelial cells and binds type IV collagen in basement membranes?
quiz_ct:20.r: Laminin: basement membranes, epithelial origin, binds type IV collagen and heparan sulfate.

quiz_ct:22.q: Which stain is most commonly used to demonstrate the thin fibers marked X?
quiz_ct:22.r: X = elastic fibers: orcein (brownish-red); do not stain with H&E.
quiz_ct:22.alt: Light micrograph of thin and thick fibers marked X and Y

quiz_ct:24.q: The aortic change on the right is seen in Marfan syndrome. The mutated protein normally forms which structure?
quiz_ct:24.r: Marfan = fibrillin mutation; fibrillin forms the microfibrils (oxytalan fibers).
quiz_ct:24.alt: Drawings of a heart with a normal aorta and an enlarged aorta

quiz_ct:27.q: A patient whose diet lacks vitamin C develops the gum changes shown. Which step of collagen synthesis is impaired?
quiz_ct:27.r: Scurvy: vitamin C is the cofactor for proline hydroxylase.

quiz_ct:28.q: A patient has the joint finding shown and frequent dislocations. Decreased activity of which enzyme explains this?
quiz_ct:28.r: Ehlers-Danlos type VII: decreased procollagen peptidase; increased articular mobility, frequent luxation.
quiz_ct:28.alt: Photograph of a hand with a finger bent far backward

quiz_ct:29.q: The dark branching fibers at the arrows are made mainly of which collagen type?
quiz_ct:29.alt: Light micrograph with arrows on thin branching fibers

quiz_ct:3.q: In which structure is the tissue shown typically found?
quiz_ct:3.r: Dense regular collagenous tissue = tendon (faculty slide 978).
quiz_ct:3.alt: Light micrograph of a pink wavy tissue with flattened nuclei

quiz_ct:30.q: Which type of stain was used to show the black fibers in this lymph node?
quiz_ct:30.r: Reticular fibers are argyrophilic: black with silver stains.
quiz_ct:30.alt: Light micrograph of a network of black fibers

quiz_ct:5.q: At the arterial end of a capillary, hydrostatic pressure exceeds the colloid osmotic pressure of plasma. What is the result?
quiz_ct:5.r: Arterial end 40 vs 25 mm Hg: fluid leaves; venous end 15 vs 25: fluid returns.

quiz_ct:6.q: Which cell is derived from the hematopoietic stem cell?
quiz_ct:6.r: Osteoclast = fused monocytes (hematopoietic); the others are mesenchymal.

quiz_ct:7.q: This is the most common cell of connective tissue. The organelle at the end of the line marked X is prominent because this cell does what?
quiz_ct:7.r: Fibroblast: rich in RER and Golgi; synthesizes fibrous and amorphous ECM.
quiz_ct:7.alt: Electron micrograph of an elongated cell with a line marked X

quiz_ct:8.q: What is a main function of the cells shown?
quiz_ct:8.r: Unilocular adipocytes: energy store, shock absorber, thermal insulation.
quiz_ct:8.alt: Light micrograph of large empty-looking cells with thin rims

quiz_ct:9.q: Compared with ordinary fat, the tissue shown is better able to perform which function?
quiz_ct:9.r: Multilocular (brown) fat: many droplets, abundant mitochondria, heat in neonates.
quiz_ct:9.alt: Light micrograph of cells filled with many small vacuoles

quiz_ct_b:1.q: Three headings are hidden on this classification chart. Which heading belongs in box Y?
quiz_ct_b:1.r: Adipose, elastic, hematopoietic and mucous tissue sit under connective tissue with special properties; loose and dense tissue are connective tissue proper, and cartilage and bone are supporting connective tissues (p. 929).
quiz_ct_b:1.alt: Classification chart of connective tissue with its three second-row headings covered and marked X, Y and Z.

quiz_ct_b:2.q: Connective tissue cells arise from either undifferentiated mesenchymal cells or hematopoietic stem cells. Which pair comes from two different lines?
quiz_ct_b:2.r: Osteoblasts come from undifferentiated mesenchymal cells, like fibroblasts, adipocytes and chondroblasts; osteoclasts come from hematopoietic stem cells, like mast cells, macrophages, plasma cells and microglia (p. 931).

quiz_ct_b:3.q: In hemidesmosomes, the two-chain membrane protein drawn here takes the place of which protein?
quiz_ct_b:3.r: The drawing is an integrin with its alpha and beta chains. The slide states that integrins replace cadherins in hemidesmosomes; laminin and fibronectin are what integrins bind (p. 951).
quiz_ct_b:3.alt: Drawing of a membrane protein made of an alpha chain and a beta chain, linked to actin inside the cell.

quiz_ct_b:4.q: These panels show three stages of elastic fiber formation. Where does the slide locate fibers of stage A, which contain fibrillin only?
quiz_ct_b:4.r: Stage A is oxytalan (fibrillin), found in the zonule fibers that connect the ciliary body to the lens; stage B is elaunin (elastin), found around sweat glands; stage C is the mature elastic fiber (p. 962).
quiz_ct_b:4.alt: Three electron micrographs marked A, B and C: fine fibrils only, fibrils with dark patches, and one large dark mass.

quiz_ct_recheck:1.q: Kupffer cells, microglia and osteoclasts all arise from which blood cell?
quiz_ct_recheck:1.r: Macrophage family comes from blood monocytes.

quiz_ct_recheck:12.q: A patient has hypermobile joints with frequent dislocations caused by decreased procollagen peptidase activity. Which step of collagen formation fails?
quiz_ct_recheck:12.r: Procollagen peptidase removes registration peptides outside the cell; EDS type VII.

quiz_ct_recheck:2.q: A cell in the lamina propria has an eccentric nucleus with cartwheel chromatin and abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum. From which cell did it arise?
quiz_ct_recheck:2.r: Plasma cell: derived from stimulated B lymphocytes.

quiz_ct_recheck:6.q: Laminin is a characteristic glycoprotein of which structure?
quiz_ct_recheck:6.r: Laminin: present in basement membranes, secreted by epithelial cells.

quiz_ct_recheck:7.q: The fine black meshwork that supports this lymphoid organ is shown with which type of stain?
quiz_ct_recheck:7.r: Reticular fibers (type III) are argyrophilic: black with silver.
quiz_ct_recheck:7.alt: Low-power micrograph of an organ with a fine black meshwork

quiz_ct_recheck:8.q: The thin dark fibers between the red collagen bundles of this dermis recoil after stretching. According to the lecture, which stain is most commonly used to show this fiber type?
quiz_ct_recheck:8.r: Elastic fibers: orcein is the most common stain.
quiz_ct_recheck:8.alt: Micrograph of skin with red bundles and thin dark fibers in the dermis

quiz_ct_recheck:9.q: The dark wavy sheets in this arterial wall stretch and recoil. They are laid down on a scaffold of microfibrils made of which protein?
quiz_ct_recheck:9.r: Elastic fibers = fibrillin microfibrils (oxytalan) + elastin; Marfan = fibrillin.
quiz_ct_recheck:9.alt: Micrograph of an arterial wall with many dark wavy layers

brief:
Connective Tissue High-Yield Tables (Exam 3)

Connective Tissue (Djakiew) was your lowest histology quiz in September at 21/43, with ground substance the weakest part at 2/7. Page numbers are pages of the combined PDF: slides pp. 924–979, handout pp. 980–990. Everything is from those pages unless labeled (outside the slides).

1. General features, origin and functions (LO 1)

Connective tissue is defined by its matrix: the extracellular matrix (ECM) predominates over the cells (p. 980).

Feature Connective tissue Contrast with epithelium
Cell packing Not closely packed Tightly packed
Polarity None Polarized
Attachment junctions None Present
Vascularity Usually well vascularized Avascular
Distribution Widespread, except the central nervous system

The epithelium column is from the Epithelium lecture, added for contrast.

Origin fact Detail (p. 980)
Germ layer Mesoderm, as mesenchyme
Mesenchyme Undifferentiated cells with minimal ECM
Role Progenitor of all connective tissue cells
In the adult Still present; replenishes the cells and is important in wound healing
Function Provided by Detail (p. 980)
Supporting framework Fibrous ECM Capsules, trabeculae, and stroma that supports the parenchyma
Transport of nutrients Amorphous ECM A polyanionic hydrophilic gel
Defense against infection Cells and amorphous ECM Three steps, below
Wound healing Fibroblasts, mesenchymal cells Best capacity to regenerate
Storage Adipose tissue

The three defense steps, in order (p. 980):

  1. Localization of the infection: more plasma leakage, higher extravascular osmotic pressure, fluid accumulation (edema)
  2. Phagocytosis by blood leukocytes and connective tissue macrophages
  3. Initiation of the immune response by lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages
Capillary end Hydrostatic pressure Colloid osmotic pressure Net fluid movement (pp. 971–972)
Arterial 40 mm Hg 25 mm Hg Out of the capillary
Venous 15 mm Hg 25 mm Hg Back into the capillary

Some of the fluid is drained by lymphatic capillaries instead (p. 972).

2. Classification (LO 1)

Type is set by which matrix component predominates and by the number and types of cells present (p. 990). The handout and the slide group the types slightly differently, so know both.

Type (handout, p. 990) Where What marks it
Loose (areolar) Mucous membranes (lamina propria), mesentery All connective tissue cell types present
Dense irregular Dermis, capsules of glands, periosteum
Dense regular, collagenous Tendons
Dense regular, elastic Yellow ligaments
Reticular Spleen, lymph nodes, bone marrow
Specialized: cartilage
Specialized: bone
Specialized: blood, hemopoietic and lymphopoietic tissue
Specialized: adipose, unilocular Widespread Single lipid droplet
Specialized: adipose, multilocular (brown fat) Mostly neonatal Multiple droplets, rich in mitochondria
Group on the slide (p. 929) Members Slide annotation
Connective tissue proper Loose Lamina propria
Connective tissue proper Dense regular Ligaments, tendons
Connective tissue proper Dense irregular Dermis
Special properties Adipose, elastic, hematopoietic, mucous Mucous tissue lines the GI, respiratory and reproductive tracts
Supporting Cartilage, bone

A mucous membrane is lining epithelium plus an underlying layer of loose connective tissue called the lamina propria. It lines cavities that open to the outside: digestive tract, airways, genitourinary tract (p. 981).

3. Cells (LO 2)

Six cell types are listed on the slide: fibroblasts, adipose cells, macrophages, mast cells, leukocytes and plasma cells (p. 934).

Cell How to spot it What it does Page
Fibroblast Oval or spindle shaped; rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) and Golgi Most common cell; makes the fibrous and amorphous matrix, such as collagen 981
Fibrocyte Drawn slimmer than the fibroblast in handout Figure 3 The inactive fibroblast 981
Unilocular adipocyte Very large (about 100 µm); one lipid droplet; nucleus and cytoplasm pushed to the edge Energy store, shock absorber, thermal insulation 981
Multilocular adipocyte Many lipid droplets; abundant mitochondria Brown fat; generates heat in neonates 939, 981
Macrophage Kidney-shaped nucleus; well-developed Golgi; abundant lysosomes Phagocytosis, antigen processing and presentation, cytokine secretion 941, 983
Plasma cell Small, oval; eccentric nucleus; cartwheel heterochromatin; abundant RER Makes immunoglobulins; derived from stimulated B lymphocytes 943, 983
Mast cell Large; perivascular; cytoplasm full of large basophilic, electron-dense granules First line of defense; allergic response 983
Lymphocyte Large nucleus, thin rim of basophilic cytoplasm Main cell of the immune response 983
Neutrophil Phagocytoses bacteria 983
Eosinophil Kills schistosome worms 983
Monocyte Gives rise to macrophages 983

Macrophages come from blood monocytes and take a different name in each tissue (p. 981).

Tissue Macrophage name
Liver Kupffer cell
Central nervous system Microglial cell
Integument Langerhans cell
Bone Osteoclast
Mast cell product Effect (p. 983) Stored or made on demand (p. 945)
Histamine Vasodilator; increases capillary permeability; bronchoconstrictor Stored in granules
Heparin Anticoagulant and lipolytic agent Stored in granules
Leukotrienes Smooth muscle contraction Made from membrane phospholipids by phospholipases

Mast cell activation (pp. 945, 983):

  1. Immunoglobulin E (IgE) binds to IgE receptors on the cell surface
  2. A second exposure to the antigen cross-links the bound IgE
  3. Calcium enters and the granules fuse and release histamine and heparin
  4. Phospholipases act on membrane phospholipids to make leukotrienes

Mast cells have a different stem cell origin from basophils (p. 983).

Stem cell Gives rise to (p. 931)
Undifferentiated mesenchymal cell Fibroblast, adipocyte, chondroblast, osteoblast, endothelial cell, mesothelial cell, smooth muscle cell
Hematopoietic stem cell Red cell, megakaryocyte, neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil, mast cell, B and T lymphocytes, plasma cell, monocyte, macrophage, osteoclast, microglia, Langerhans cell

The trap in that table is the bone pair: the osteoblast is mesenchymal, the osteoclast is hematopoietic (fused monocytes, p. 973).

4. Ground substance (LO 3)

Ground substance is about 10% of the matrix by weight but fills about 90% of its volume (p. 985). The matrix is secreted mainly by fibroblasts.

Component What it is Key facts Page
Glycosaminoglycan (GAG) Long unbranched chain of repeating disaccharides; one sugar is always an amino sugar Binds large amounts of water; forms a polyanionic hydrated gel 947, 985
Proteoglycan GAGs covalently bound to a central core protein; bottle-brush shape More than 90% carbohydrate by weight 949, 985
Proteoglycan aggregate Proteoglycans attached to hyaluronic acid by link proteins Hyaluronan is the axis; the link protein joins the core protein to it 948, 985
Glycoprotein Globular protein with short, branched monosaccharide chains Mostly protein; promotes cell attachment to the matrix 949, 985

The amino sugar is N-acetylglucosamine or N-acetylgalactosamine (p. 985). The hydrated gel allows rapid diffusion of water-soluble molecules and lets cells migrate during development and wound healing.

Feature Hyaluronic acid All other GAGs
Sulfation Not sulfated Highly sulfated
Core protein Not attached to one Attached as side branches
Size Very large; occupies a huge volume Not stated
Role in aggregates The central axis The bristles on each proteoglycan
GAG Where it is found (handout Table I, p. 986)
Hyaluronic acid Umbilical cord, synovial fluid, vitreous humor, cartilage
Chondroitin 4-sulfate Cartilage, bone, cornea, skin, notochord, aorta
Chondroitin 6-sulfate Cartilage, umbilical cord, skin, aorta (media)
Dermatan sulfate Skin, tendon, aorta (adventitia)
Heparan sulfate Aorta, lung, liver, basal laminae
Keratan sulfate Cornea; cartilage, nucleus pulposus, annulus fibrosus
Glycoprotein Made by Shape Binding domains Page
Fibronectin Fibroblasts, primarily Dimer Plasma membrane, heparan sulfate, collagen 950, 985
Laminin Epithelial cells Trimer Plasma membrane, heparan sulfate, type IV collagen 950, 985

Laminin is the one found in basement membranes (p. 985).

Integrin fact Detail Page
Job Transmembrane link from the cytoskeleton to the matrix 985
Subunits 16 alpha and 8 beta 985
Alpha subunit Sets which matrix molecule is bound 985
Beta subunit Mediates the link to the cytoskeleton 985
α5β1 Binds fibronectin 951
α6β4 Binds laminin 951
Hemidesmosomes Integrins replace cadherins 951

5. Collagen (LO 3)

Collagen is the major body protein, type I is the most common, and it stains with acid dyes, so it is eosinophilic (p. 987).

Level What it is Page
Tropocollagen The basic unit: three alpha chains held by hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions; 280 nm long 986–987
Fibril Staggered tropocollagen units 987
Fiber Bundled fibrils 954
Fiber bundle Bundled fibers 954
Banding fact Detail (pp. 986–987)
Period 64 nm (640 Å), from the staggered arrangement
Dark bands Gap (lacunar) regions between tropocollagen units
Why dark The gaps fill with glycoproteins and proteoglycans, which are electron dense
Light bands Overlapping regions with no gaps

Hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine are the characteristic amino acids. Their hydroxylation depends on vitamin C and is essential for mechanical strength (p. 987).

Synthesis, in order (pp. 954, 989):

  1. Nucleus: messenger RNA for each type of alpha chain
  2. RER: alpha chains of preprocollagen made with registration peptides; signal peptide clipped
  3. RER: hydroxylation of specific prolyl and lysyl residues (vitamin C dependent)
  4. RER: galactosyl and glucosyl sugars attached to hydroxylysyl residues
  5. Procollagen triple helix assembles
  6. Golgi packages procollagen into secretory vesicles
  7. Vesicles move to the cell surface along microtubules and microfilaments
  8. Outside the cell: procollagen peptidases cleave the registration peptides, giving insoluble tropocollagen
  9. Tropocollagen aggregates into fibrils
  10. Lysyl oxidase makes covalent cross-links that reinforce the fibril
Collagen type Key fact Page
I Most common 987
II The cartilage collagen 988
III Forms reticular fibers 952, 990
IV Keeps its registration peptide, so no fibrils and no banding; laminin binds it 985, 988
VII Long chains; attaches the basement membrane to the underlying stroma 988
IX and XI Minor collagens with type II in cartilage; stabilize the type II network 988
Disorder Defect Result Page
Ehlers-Danlos type IV Faulty transcription or translation of type III Aortic or intestinal rupture 957
Ehlers-Danlos type VI Faulty lysine hydroxylation Very elastic skin, rupture of the eyeball 957
Ehlers-Danlos type VII Decreased procollagen peptidase activity Increased joint mobility, frequent dislocation 957
Scurvy Lack of vitamin C, the cofactor for proline hydroxylase Ulcerated gums, hemorrhages 957–958
Osteogenesis imperfecta One-nucleotide change in type I collagen genes Spontaneous fractures, cardiac insufficiency 957
Collagen function Slide wording (p. 953)
Adhesion Discrete and restricted to cells and tissues
Skeletal Established in vertebrates
Protective Dermis (leather)
Messenger Acts on cell behavior

There are more than 20 collagen types (p. 953). Collagen recovered from a 68-million-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex bone was most similar to that of birds (pp. 960, 988).

6. Elastic and reticular fibers (LO 3)

The three fibers are told apart by their protein and their stain (p. 952).

Feature Collagen fibers Reticular fibers Elastic fibers
Made of Type I collagen mostly Type III collagen Fibrillin microfibrils plus elastin
Stain Acid dyes; eosinophilic Silver, black (argyrophilic); also PAS Orcein, brownish-red; aldehyde fuchsin
With H&E Pink Do not stain
Under the electron microscope Banded fibrils Thinner fibrils: about 30–40 nm, against 60–90 nm for type I (p. 970) Electron lucent
Job Mechanical strength Delicate supporting network Stretch and recoil
Where Tendon, dermis, mesentery Bone marrow, lymph nodes, spleen, liver; embryo; wound healing Vessel walls as fenestrated membranes; yellow ligaments
Page 955, 987 966, 970, 990 963, 990

PAS is the periodic acid–Schiff stain. "Delicate supporting network" is my shorthand for the reticular row; the handout gives only the composition and the sites.

Reticular fiber fact Detail (p. 990)
Packing Tropocollagen units packed loosely
Spaces Filled with more proteoglycans and glycoproteins: 6–12%, against 1% in type I
Enriched in Lymphoid organs and tissues (p. 966)
Elastic fiber part Protein Property Page
Microfibrils (oxytalan fibers) Fibrillin, a glycoprotein Resist tension 962, 990
Amorphous core Elastin Cross-linked network that stretches and recoils 964, 990

Elastin is marked by two amino acids, desmosine and isodesmosine (p. 990).

Stage of elastic fiber formation Labeled on the slide as Slide example (p. 962)
Oxytalan Fibrillin Zonule fibers connecting the ciliary body to the lens
Elaunin Elastin Around sweat glands
Elastic fiber Mature fiber
Clinical or evolution fact Detail Page
Marfan syndrome Inherited mutation in the fibrillin gene 965
First appearance of elastin With closed, high-pressure circulatory systems 961
Which animals have elastin Jawed vertebrates (gnathostomes); not jawless fish or invertebrates 961

7. What the lecture's own practice questions tested

The six practice questions at the end of the slides are faculty-written, so they show what he considers testable (pp. 973–978). Five of the six are image identification.

Slide What it asked Answer on the slide
973 Which cell is derived from hematopoietic stem cells Osteoclast (fused monocytes)
974 Identify the cell in an image Plasma cell
975 Identify the cells in an image Unilocular adipocytes
976 Identify the matrix component in an image Collagen fibers
977 Identify the cell in an image Macrophage
978 Classify the tissue in an image Dense regular (tendon)

One key to double-check: the slide 974 answer reads "E (abundant SER)", meaning smooth endoplasmic reticulum. The lecture slide and the handout both say the plasma cell has abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum (pp. 943, 983). The answer, plasma cell, is right either way. If an exam option forces the choice, go with rough, since two of his three sources say it.

8. Your September misses

You missed 22 of 43 on the first quiz. These are those items, each with its rule.

Area The fact you missed Page
Ground substance About 10% of matrix weight but about 90% of its volume 985
Ground substance Hyaluronic acid is the only non-sulfated GAG 985
Ground substance The link protein attaches the core protein to hyaluronan 948
Ground substance Laminin is found in basement membranes 985
Ground substance Integrin alpha sets matrix specificity; beta links to the cytoskeleton 985
Classification and function Adult mesenchymal cells replenish connective tissue cells and aid wound healing 980
Classification and function The osteoclast is fused monocytes 973
Classification and function Loose areolar tissue has all the cell types; lamina propria and mesentery 990
Classification and function First defense step is localization, by edema from plasma leakage 980
Cells Histamine raises vessel permeability 983
Cells The inactive fibroblast is the fibrocyte 981
Cells Fibroblast RER makes the matrix proteins 981
Cells Plasma cell has cartwheel chromatin 943
Cells Leukotrienes cause smooth muscle contraction 983
Collagen Collagen is eosinophilic; it takes acid dyes 987
Collagen Dark bands are the gap regions, filled with proteoglycans 987
Collagen Ehlers-Danlos type VII is low procollagen peptidase 957
Collagen Type IV keeps its registration peptide, so no banding 988
Elastic fibers Orcein stains elastic fibers 963
Elastic fibers Desmosine and isodesmosine cross-link elastin 990
Elastic fibers Oxytalan (fibrillin microfibrils) resists tension 990
Elastic fibers Marfan syndrome is a fibrillin mutation 965

Two repeat misses from other lectures belong here too: hemidesmosomes use integrins, not cadherins (p. 951), and anchoring fibrils are type VII collagen (p. 988).
